title: The Seventeenth of Tammuz
hook: a fast for the breach of Jerusalem's walls, beginning the Three Weeks

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shavuot, with blintzes and branches. Your line was green and milk. Did something green come inside? Today the calendar turns, from harvest toward mourning. Day six hundred ninety-three.

Yom Kippur and the ninth of Av, the two long Jewish fasts, begin at sunset. This one begins at dawn. On a summer morning, while it's still dark, some people are up eating a quick breakfast and drinking as much water as they can. Then nothing, no food, no drink, until the stars come out. It's a long day at the height of summer. There's no special meal at the end, no famous melody, no crowd. Plenty of people walk past the date without noticing. But in the synagogue, the Torah is read and extra prayers are said, and a season has started. The day remembers a wall.
screen: `A FAST FROM DAWN.` → `A LONG SUMMER DAY.` → `IT REMEMBERS A WALL.`

segments.voice: Tammuz is a summer month in the Hebrew calendar, and on its seventeenth day the Mishnah gathers a run of disasters. It lists five. Moses broke the tablets, coming down the mountain to find the golden calf. The daily offering in the Temple stopped. The walls of Jerusalem were breached. A man called Apostomus burned a Torah scroll. And an idol was set up in the sanctuary. Some of these we can place; some we can't. Nobody is sure who Apostomus was. The walls bring a puzzle of their own. The book of Jeremiah says that when the Babylonians broke into Jerusalem, it was on the ninth of the month, not the seventeenth. The Talmud notices this, and answers that the seventeenth belongs to the second wall, when the Romans broke in centuries later. The Jerusalem Talmud offers another answer: in the chaos, people lost track of the date. Either way, the fast keeps the breach, and the reason is worth sitting with. A city doesn't fall the day its walls are breached. It falls weeks later. The breach is the day the danger gets inside, the first crack. So this fast opens a season. Three weeks from today is the ninth of Av, the day both Temples are remembered as destroyed. The weeks in between have a name from the book of Lamentations, bein hametzarim, between the narrow places. The fast itself runs from dawn to nightfall, and like the other minor fasts it excuses anyone ill, pregnant or nursing. Customs vary: some communities hold no weddings in these weeks, play less music, and some people don't cut their hair. And there's a promise attached. The prophet Zechariah says the fast of the fourth month, which is this one, will one day become a time of joy and gladness. Even the mourning is kept with an eye on mending.
screen: `FIVE DISASTERS, ONE DATE.` · `WHICH WALL? THE ROMANS' BREACH.` · `THE CRACK COMES FIRST.` · `THREE WEEKS IN THE NARROW PLACES.` · then, large: `WALLS BREACHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one crack that needs mending. Sit still and let your breathing slow. Then walk, in your mind, around the walls of your life: a friendship, your health, your work, your home, the way you speak to someone close. Don't fix anything yet. Just look for the place where something small has started to give: a message you keep not answering, a resentment that's grown a little, a habit slipping. When you find one, stay with it gently. Name it. That's all. Noticing early is the work. The bell holds the time.
Bein hametzarim. Between the narrow places: the three weeks of mourning that open with the fast for the breach of Jerusalem's walls.
Your line: walls breached. Today, take one small step on the crack you found: a text, an apology, a repair, a doctor's appointment you've been putting off. Day six hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: On the Seventeenth of Tammuz observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall, with a special Torah reading and added prayers; it begins the Three Weeks, when some communities hold no weddings and limit music until Tisha B'Av.

original.note: Hebrew: the seventeenth of Tammuz, the fourth month counting from Nisan.

notes: Added 2026-10-06 from the five-year map (standing rule: every fast-day lesson carries the health line; never present fasting as required at risk to health): one sentence that health and life come first. Minor fasts (Tenth of Tevet, Fast of Esther, Seventeenth of Tammuz): the ill, pregnant and nursing are generally excused (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 550:1 and 686:2 with commentaries). Tisha B'Av: the ill and anyone at risk eat; others ask a doctor and a rabbi (OC 554:5-6). Confirm with the Keeper.
Five events of 17 Tammuz from Mishnah Taanit 4:6, order as listed there. Identity of Apostomus is uncertain; stated as such.

Babylonian Talmud Taanit 28b resolves Jeremiah 39:2 (ninth of the fourth month) by assigning the seventeenth to the Second Temple; the Jerusalem Talmud (Taanit 4:5, check numbering) says the date was miscounted amid the troubles. Verify both.
Three Weeks customs (no weddings, limited music, some refrain from haircuts) vary by community; the haircut custom is mainly Ashkenazi.
'Bein hametzarim' from Lamentations 1:3; rendered 'between the narrow places' as a paraphrase.
Zechariah 8:19 calls it the fast of the fourth month; identification with 17 Tammuz is the traditional reading.
The date falls between late June and late July in the civil calendar.

Review pass: the hook originally said 'most Jewish fasts begin at sunset', which is inaccurate (only Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av run sunset to nightfall; the minor fasts run dawn to nightfall). Reworded to name the two sunset fasts.
